title: Restated, copied or off topic?
instructions: Thesis: “Our school should start a community garden because it teaches science, improves meals and brings students together.” Sort each possible first sentence of the conclusion.

items.text: A school garden would turn our lessons, our lunches and our friendships into something better.
Growing a garden would help students learn science, eat well and work together.
Our school should start a community garden because it teaches science, improves meals and brings students together.
Our school should start a community garden because it teaches science, improves meals and brings students together!
Our school also needs a bigger library.
In conclusion, that is the end of my essay.

title: Say it again, differently
instructions: Choose the words that restate each thesis without copying it.

items.sentence: Thesis: “Our school should start a garden.” Restated: A garden is a ___ our school should make.
items.hint: Which words say the same idea in a new way?

items.sentence: Thesis: “Sleep affects learning in three ways.” Restated: Sleep shapes ___ students learn.
items.explanation: “Sleep shapes how well students learn” keeps the focus in new words.

items.sentence: Thesis: “Students should choose their own clothes.” Restated: Students deserve the ___ to decide what they wear.
items.hint: Which word turns “choose” into a new phrase?
items.explanation: “The freedom to decide” restates “choose” without copying.

questions.prompt: What is the first job of a conclusion?

options.text: Restate the thesis in new words

questions.explanation: The conclusion reminds the reader of the main point.

questions.prompt: Why not copy the thesis word for word?

options.text: It sounds repetitive and shows nothing new
It makes the essay too long

questions.explanation: New words show you understand your own point.

questions.prompt: Which is the weakest way to start a conclusion?

options.text: In conclusion, this was my essay about gardens.
A garden would make our school healthier and happier.
Growing food together would change our school for the better.

questions.explanation: Announcing the end says nothing about the thesis.

title: Three restatements
prompt: Restate each thesis in new words, the way you would at the start of a conclusion.
tips: Keep the same claim or focus, with a claim word like should, deserve, need or better.
Change the words: swap synonyms, change the order, combine the reasons.

sentences.ask: Thesis: “Our school should start a community garden because it teaches science, improves meals and brings students together.”
Thesis: “Students should be allowed to choose their own clothes because it saves families money, lets students stay comfortable and encourages self-expression.”
Thesis: “Every student should learn to swim because it builds confidence and saves lives.”

title: A strong ending?
instructions: Sort each last sentence of a conclusion.

items.text: Let’s ask the principal for a small plot of land this spring.
Imagine a lunch line full of food we grew ourselves.
If we start today, next year’s students will thank us.
That is all I have to say.
Thank you for reading my essay.
Also, gardens need water.

title: Build a conclusion
instructions: Put the sentences in order: restated thesis, summary, final thought.

items.text: A community garden would make our school a better place to learn and eat.
It would turn science lessons into real experiments and put fresh food on our plates.
Most of all, it would give students a reason to work together.
Let’s ask the principal for a small plot of land this spring.

explanation: Restate → sum up the main points → leave the reader with a final thought.

questions.prompt: What does the summary in a conclusion do?

options.text: Reminds the reader of the main points in a sentence or two

questions.explanation: Short and complete: just the main points.

questions.prompt: Which is a call to action?

options.text: Write to the school board this week and ask for a garden.

questions.explanation: A call to action asks the reader to do something.

questions.prompt: What should a conclusion NOT do?
questions.explanation: New reasons belong in body paragraphs.

title: Write a conclusion
prompt: Thesis: “Students should be allowed to choose their own clothes because it saves families money, lets students stay comfortable and encourages self-expression.” Write the conclusion of this argumentative essay: restate the thesis in new words, sum up the three reasons in a sentence or two, and end with a final thought (a call to act, a look ahead or a question). One paragraph.
tips: Restate: say the claim again in new words. Don’t copy the thesis.
Summary: money, comfort, self-expression.
Final thought: “Let’s…”, “Imagine…”, “If we…, then…”.

essay.thesis: Students should be allowed to choose their own clothes because it saves families money, lets students stay comfortable and encourages self-expression.

title: Where does it go?
instructions: An informative essay explains how honeybees help farms. Sort each sentence into the part of the essay it belongs in.

items.text: Did you know that one in three bites of food depends on pollinators?
Honeybees help farms in three ways: they pollinate crops, make honey and support wildlife.
As bees feed, they carry pollen from flower to flower on their legs.
A strong hive can make more than 25 kilograms of honey in a year.
Without honeybees, farms would grow less food, earn less money and host less wildlife.
Next time you eat an apple, thank a bee.

questions.prompt: How many body paragraphs does an informative essay with a three-part thesis need?
questions.explanation: One body paragraph per part.

questions.prompt: What does an informative conclusion leave the reader with?

options.text: Why the topic matters, or something to look out for
A new part to learn about

questions.explanation: Explain, then leave a final thought.

questions.prompt: Which hook suits an informative essay about volcanoes?

options.text: Every day, about 20 volcanoes are erupting somewhere on Earth.
In this essay I will talk about volcanoes.

questions.explanation: A surprising fact suits an informative essay.

title: Order the essay
instructions: Put the first sentences of each paragraph in order to build an informative essay.

items.text: Volcanoes form in three stages: magma rises, pressure builds and the volcano erupts.
First, hot magma rises from deep inside the Earth.
Next, pressure builds as gas gets trapped in the magma.
Finally, the pressure bursts out in an eruption.
From rising magma to a roaring eruption, a volcano grows in three powerful steps.

explanation: The body paragraphs follow the order of the thesis; the conclusion restates it in new words.

title: Write an informative essay
prompt: Write an informative essay that explains how a pet changes a family’s daily life (or choose another topic you know well: a sport, a hobby, a place). Use the outline builder to plan, press “Start my essay from the outline”, then write: an introduction (hook, background, thesis naming three parts), three body paragraphs with facts and examples, and a conclusion that restates and ends with a final thought. Check your essay map as you go.
tips: Thesis: “… in three ways: …, … and ….”
Each body paragraph explains one part, with a fact or an example.
Explain, don’t argue: no “should”.

title: Reflection words
instructions: Choose the words that turn the last sentence into a reflection.

items.sentence: That day, I ___ that being brave doesn’t mean not being scared.
items.hint: Which word shows what the writer understood?

items.sentence: ___ that summer, I have never been afraid to ask for help.
items.hint: Which words show a lasting change?
items.explanation: “Ever since” shows how the writer changed.

items.sentence: ___ I understand why my grandmother kept every letter.
items.hint: Which word looks back from today?
items.explanation: “Now I understand” reflects on the past.

title: A narrative essay
instructions: Put the first sentences of each paragraph in order to build a narrative essay.

items.text: The day I forgot my lines in the school play taught me to laugh at myself.
At first, everything went perfectly in the first scene.
Then, in the middle of my big speech, my mind went completely blank.
Suddenly, I started laughing, and the audience laughed with me.
Ever since that night, I have known that a mistake is not the end of the world.

explanation: A narrative essay tells the events in order, then reflects on what they meant.

questions.prompt: What does a narrative essay’s conclusion do?

options.text: Reflects on what the experience taught or changed

questions.explanation: A reflection gives the story its meaning.

questions.prompt: How is a narrative essay different from a short story?

options.text: It is true, and it says what the experience meant

questions.explanation: A narrative essay is a true story with a focus.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest focus for a narrative essay?

options.text: Losing the final match taught me that effort matters more than winning.

questions.explanation: A focus names what the experience meant.

title: Write a narrative essay
prompt: Write a narrative essay about a time something didn’t go as planned, and what it taught you. Use the outline builder to plan, press “Start my essay from the outline”, then write: an introduction that ends with your focus, two or three body paragraphs that tell the events in order with time words and details, and a conclusion that reflects on what you learned.
tips: Focus: “The day … taught me …”.
Time words: At first, Then, Suddenly, After that, Finally.
Reflection: “I learned…”, “Ever since…”, “Now I understand…”.

title: Plan the argument
instructions: Thesis: “Students should be allowed to choose their own clothes because it saves families money, lets students stay comfortable and encourages self-expression.” Sort each note into the part of the plan it belongs in.

items.text: Choosing clothes saves families money.
Students stay comfortable in any weather.
A full uniform can cost more than $200 a year.
For example, students could wear shorts on hot days.
Some people argue that uniforms stop bullying about clothes.
However, students are teased about shoes and bags even with uniforms.

title: Order the outline
instructions: Put the lines of this argumentative essay outline in order.

items.text: Hook: Imagine shivering through a winter day in a thin uniform skirt.
Thesis: Students should be allowed to choose their own clothes because it saves families money, lets students stay comfortable and encourages self-expression.
Body 1: Choosing clothes saves families money.
Body 2: Students stay comfortable in any weather.
Counterclaim: Some people argue that uniforms stop bullying.
Rebuttal: However, students are teased about shoes and bags anyway.
Conclusion: Let students choose, and let the school focus on learning.

explanation: Hook and thesis → reasons with evidence → the other side and your answer → conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why plan an essay before writing it?

options.text: So every paragraph has a job and the order makes sense
Because planning is faster than writing
So you can skip the conclusion

questions.explanation: A plan keeps the essay focused.

questions.prompt: Where does the counterclaim usually go?

options.text: After the reasons, before the conclusion

questions.explanation: Prove your side, then answer the other side.

questions.prompt: What should each body point in an outline have?
questions.explanation: Every reason needs evidence.

title: Plan an argumentative essay
prompt: Should students be allowed to choose their own clothes for school? Plan an argumentative essay on this question with the outline builder: a hook, your thesis, two reasons each with evidence, a counterclaim with your rebuttal, and your conclusion. Then press “Put it in my writing” and check your essay map.
tips: Pick your side first; your thesis can agree or disagree.
Evidence ideas: cost, comfort, weather, self-expression, school spirit.
The counterclaim is the strongest argument for the other side.

title: Link the paragraphs
instructions: Choose the transition that starts each paragraph of an argumentative essay.

items.hint: Which word starts the first reason?

items.sentence: ___, students stay comfortable in any weather.

items.hint: Which words bring in the other side?

items.sentence: ___, letting students choose would make school fairer and happier.

questions.prompt: What makes an argumentative essay convincing?

options.text: Reasons backed by evidence, and an answer to the other side
Using capital letters for important words

questions.explanation: Evidence and a rebuttal win readers over.

questions.prompt: Which tone suits an argumentative essay?
questions.explanation: Respect the other side while you answer it.

questions.prompt: How do you use the essay checklist?

options.text: Edit until every item is done, then read it aloud
Ignore it until the end of the year

questions.explanation: The checklist guides your editing.

title: Fix it or keep it?
instructions: While editing an argumentative essay, sort each sentence: keep it, or fix it.

items.text: According to a parent survey, uniforms cost families $200 a year.
This shows that choosing clothes would save families money.
However, students are teased about shoes and bags even with uniforms.
In this essay I will talk about uniforms.
Uniforms are bad and stuff.
Some people say uniforms stop bullying.

title: Write an argumentative essay
prompt: Should students be allowed to choose their own clothes for school? Write your argumentative essay: use the outline builder (or your plan from the last lesson), press “Start my essay from the outline”, then write five paragraphs: introduction, two body paragraphs with evidence, a counterclaim paragraph with your rebuttal, and a conclusion. Edit with the essay checklist until every item is done.
tips: Each body paragraph: topic sentence → evidence → explanation.
Counterclaim: Some people argue… However, …
Conclusion: restate, sum up, final thought.

items.text: Each part has its own paragraph: introduction, body paragraphs, conclusion.
My introduction opens with a hook.
My introduction ends with a clear thesis.
Every body paragraph starts with a topic sentence that links to my thesis.
Every body paragraph has evidence: a fact, an example or a quote.
I give the other side and answer it.
My conclusion restates my thesis in new words.
My conclusion ends with a final thought.
The Coach finds no grammar or punctuation mistakes.
I explained every piece of evidence (This shows that…).
I used transitions to move between paragraphs.
I replaced vague words like good, bad, things and stuff.
I read my essay aloud and fixed anything that sounded wrong.

title: Conclusions & Full Essays check
instructions: Ten questions on everything in this unit. You need 8 or more right (80%) to pass. If you don’t pass, you’ll see what to review and get new questions to try again.

questions.prompt: What does a conclusion start with?

options.text: The thesis restated in new words

questions.explanation: Remind the reader of the main point first.

questions.prompt: Thesis: “Schools should have longer lunch breaks because students need rest and time to eat.” Which restates it?

options.text: A longer lunch would give students the rest and food they need.
Schools should have longer lunch breaks because students need rest and time to eat.

questions.explanation: Same claim, new words.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with “In conclusion, I have told you about lunch”?

options.text: It announces instead of restating the thesis

questions.explanation: Restate the claim; don’t announce the end.

questions.prompt: Why restate the thesis instead of copying it?

options.text: New words sound fresh and show you understand your point

questions.explanation: Copying sounds repetitive.

questions.prompt: What comes after the restated thesis?

options.text: A short summary of the main points

questions.explanation: Restate → summary → final thought.

questions.prompt: Which is a strong final thought?

options.text: Imagine a school where every student has time to eat and rest.

questions.explanation: “Imagine…” leaves the reader thinking.

questions.prompt: Which is a call to action?

options.text: Ask your principal for a longer lunch break this week.

questions.explanation: A call to action asks the reader to do something.

questions.prompt: What should a conclusion never add?

options.text: A new reason that wasn’t in the essay

questions.explanation: New reasons belong in body paragraphs.

questions.prompt: How many body paragraphs for a thesis with three parts?
questions.explanation: One body paragraph per part.

questions.prompt: Which thesis suits an informative essay?

options.text: Recycling works in three steps: collecting, sorting and remaking.

questions.explanation: Informative theses name the parts; they don’t argue.

questions.prompt: What do informative body paragraphs use?
questions.explanation: Explain with accurate information.

questions.prompt: Which is a good final thought for an informative essay about recycling?

options.text: Next time you toss a bottle, picture its journey to a new life.
In this essay I explained recycling.

questions.explanation: A look ahead leaves the reader thinking.

questions.prompt: What ends a narrative essay?

options.text: A reflection on what the experience taught or changed

questions.explanation: Reflect on the meaning.

questions.prompt: What keeps a narrative essay’s events clear?

options.text: Time words like First, Then, Finally

questions.explanation: Time words show the order.

questions.prompt: Which is a reflection?

options.text: Ever since that day, I check the weather before every hike.
Some people argue hiking is dangerous.

questions.explanation: “Ever since” shows a lasting change.

questions.prompt: Where does a narrative essay’s focus go?

options.text: At the end of the introduction
In the middle of the last body paragraph

questions.explanation: Like a thesis, the focus ends the introduction.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in writing an argumentative essay?

options.text: Choose your side and plan your reasons

questions.explanation: Plan, draft, then check.

questions.prompt: In an outline, what goes under each body point?
questions.explanation: Every reason needs evidence.

questions.prompt: Where does the counterclaim go in a five-paragraph argumentative essay?

options.text: The fourth paragraph, after the two reasons

questions.explanation: Reasons first, then the other side, then the conclusion.

questions.prompt: What does the essay checklist help you do?

options.text: Edit your essay part by part

questions.explanation: Use it to check each part.

questions.prompt: Which sentence should be fixed while editing?

options.text: In this essay I will talk about lunch.
A longer lunch would help students focus in the afternoon.
However, a longer break would not shorten lessons much.

questions.explanation: Replace announcements with a hook or a thesis.

questions.prompt: What makes a counterclaim paragraph strong?

options.text: A fair counterclaim and a rebuttal with evidence

questions.explanation: Answer the other side with evidence.

questions.prompt: Which transition starts the conclusion?
questions.explanation: “In the end” signals the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why read your essay aloud when editing?

options.text: You hear missing words and sentences that don’t flow

questions.explanation: Your ear catches what your eyes skip.

title: Write and edit an argumentative essay
prompt: Should students have a longer lunch break? Write an argumentative essay of five paragraphs: an introduction (hook, background, thesis), two body paragraphs with evidence and explanations, a counterclaim paragraph with your rebuttal, and a conclusion (restate, sum up, final thought). Plan with the outline builder if it helps. Then edit with the essay checklist until every item is done, and submit.
tips: Ideas: time to eat slowly, rest before afternoon lessons, time to play and make friends, clubs at lunch.
Counterclaim ideas: a longer day, less learning time.
Use the checklist: it ticks the parts it can check as you write.

items.text: Each part has its own paragraph: introduction, body paragraphs, conclusion.
My introduction opens with a hook.
My introduction ends with a clear thesis.
Every body paragraph starts with a topic sentence that links to my thesis.
Every body paragraph has evidence: a fact, an example or a quote.
I give the other side and answer it.
My conclusion restates my thesis in new words.
My conclusion ends with a final thought.
The Coach finds no grammar or punctuation mistakes.
I explained every piece of evidence (This shows that…).
I used transitions to move between paragraphs.
I replaced vague words like good, bad, things and stuff.
I read my essay aloud and fixed anything that sounded wrong.
